findings.title: Findings converge on D1's return-value outcome threading
findings.why_it_matters: Three separate findings hit the same mechanism: D1-A, where each settle step hands its outcome back up the call stack as a return value. Finding 2: a raise after outcomes are decided (reconcile, `gather_all`) unwinds the frame that holds them, so D5's "Kept" row is false. Finding 3: several paths finish with no outcome at all (config/class-load errors, `create_single_instance`'s swallowed failure, a manifest that vanished under the lock), and an empty list maps to 200. Finding 4: reload produces two outcomes per index (stop half, create half) with no rule for combining them, and the `AppBlockedError` raised after the stop half throws the stop outcomes away. Each finding's local fix adds another rule to the threading: a try/except per level, a fan-out per early return, a merge order per reload. The question for the user is whether the threading itself needs re-evaluating before it gets patched three ways. That covers whether D1's own "Pick B" condition is already met, whether "exactly one outcome per targeted index" should be a single invariant enforced in one place instead of per path, and whether some of these failure modes are better accepted and documented than handled.
findings.recommended: A: Re-evaluate D1's return-value threading before addressing Findings 2, 3 and 4 individually. Open questions: is D1's Pick-B condition met; should "one outcome per targeted index" be a single enforced invariant; which of the converging failure modes (post-decision raise, missing-outcome paths, reload's two halves, the blocked-after-stop path) are worth handling and which are limitations to accept.
findings.chosen: A: Re-evaluate D1's return-value threading before addressing Findings 2, 3 and 4 individually
findings.choice_reason: Re-evaluate, and also run prior art on how peers carry outcomes internally; 'internal' is not a reason to skip prior art. Settled: per-request collector (D1) and create-half-decides reload merge (D6).

findings.title: D5's "outcomes decided before the raise: Kept" is false under D1's return-value threading
findings.why_it_matters: D5-A promises that outcomes decided before an unexpected raise survive and only undecided targets become `failed`. Under D1-A those outcomes are local return values in frames the exception unwinds. If post-ready reconciliation raises in `initialize_instances`, every instance (already RUNNING, already announced) is reported `failed` with the reconcile message. A raise from one `stop_one` inside `gather_all` loses the sibling stops' outcomes. The two ratified decisions contradict each other as written.
findings.recommended: B: Accept as a known limitation: an unexpected raise after outcomes are decided reports every target without a surviving outcome as `failed`, and D5's "Kept" row is reworded to match.
findings.chosen: Superseded by Finding 1

findings.title: Several start/stop paths end with no outcome, and an empty outcome list maps to 200
findings.why_it_matters: D15 promises the body always lists every instance, but worst-outcome-wins over an empty list is 200. Several existing paths record no outcome. `_start_app_unlocked` catches config and class errors from `create_instances`, logs, and returns. Class-load failure records only `to_create[0]`, so a 3-instance app lists one `failed` and two missing. `create_single_instance` swallows validation errors and returns None, and `_create_instance_unlocked` discovers the failure by `registry.get(...) is None`, which is the registry inference D1 says it removes. A manifest that disappears under the lock (`_resolve_manifest` returning None after `_admit_start` parked) and "Cannot stop app, not found" both return nothing. A bad config would answer 200 "success" with `outcomes: []`.
findings.recommended: A: State the invariant "every targeted index gets exactly one outcome per request" in the ledger. Have class-load and config failures fan out to every `to_create` index, make `create_single_instance` return its outcome, answer `app_not_found` when the manifest vanished under the lock, and add these to D1's signature inventory.
findings.chosen: Superseded by Finding 1

findings.title: Reload's per-index outcome merge is unspecified, and the blocked-after-stop path drops the stop outcomes
findings.why_it_matters: Reload runs a stop half and a create half on the same index under one lock, so it yields two outcomes for one index, and the ledger lists one entry per instance without saying how they combine. If the stop half flags the index (newly flagged → 500), the create half immediately refuses it via `refusal_for`, and a naive last-wins merge reports `refused` (409) for a failure this request caused. If the stop half times out restart-safe (`failed`) and the create half succeeds, a worst-wins merge answers 500 while the new instance is running. Separately, `AppBlockedError` is raised by `_start_app_unlocked` after the stop half has run and is re-raised past the catch, so the route answers `app_blocked` with no outcomes even though instances were stopped. That contradicts the Summary's claim that `app_blocked` answers "before any instance is acted on". The route has no `app_blocked` pre-check; the code comes only from the lifecycle exception.
findings.recommended: B: The create half decides the index's outcome, except a stop half that newly flags the index, which stands as `failed` + `needs_restart`. A restart-safe stop failure followed by a good create is `succeeded` with the stop failure in `reason`. Handle the blocked path as above.
findings.chosen: Superseded by Finding 1

findings.title: Partly successful actions report as 409/500 errors whose per-instance outcomes two of three callers can't see
findings.why_it_matters: Under D3 and D15, a bulk stop or reload where siblings really did stop answers 409 or 500, with the per-instance record only in `ProblemDetail.outcomes`. The CLI's `handle_http_error` prints only `detail`. The frontend toast shows only the error message ("Failed to stop 'x': …"). So "the body lists every instance" is unreachable for two of three callers. The Summary's "restart-required text reaches the toast through the problem `detail`" is an unstated requirement on how `detail` is composed: nothing says `detail` must name which instances were refused or failed and what the rest did. A user clicks "Stop app", sees a failure toast, and can't tell that two of three instances stopped.
findings.recommended: B: Add the `detail` composition rule only.
findings.chosen: B: Add the `detail` composition rule only

findings.title: `stop` no longer converges, which contradicts the client's published retry guidance
findings.why_it_matters: `HassetteClient.action`'s docstring says "Sending `start` or `stop` again is safe, since each converges on a state". Under D3-A, a stop of an app with a flagged index answers 409 `needs_restart` every time until hassette restarts. The design changes the docstring only generically. `NeedsRestartError` will sit in the 409 family, where `BootstrapNotReleasedError` is documented "Worth retrying later", so a caller that treats a 409 as transient loops on a permanent condition, and `hassette app stop X && …` can never succeed. Changing the parent class has a cost too: released clients already map any unknown 409 code to `ConflictError`, and `AppBlockedError`, also permanent, is already a `ConflictError`.
findings.recommended: A: Keep `NeedsRestartError` under `ConflictError`. Name the doc change explicitly in the ledger: the class docstring says it isn't retryable and persists until hassette restarts, and `action`'s convergence sentence excludes a needs-restart index.
findings.chosen: A: Keep `NeedsRestartError` under `ConflictError`. Name the doc change explicitly in the ledger: the class docstring says it isn't retryable and persists until hassette restarts, and `action`'s convergence sentence excludes a needs-restart index.

findings.title: "Newly flagged" isn't available at the call sites, and the "every writer holds the lock" assumption is false at exit
findings.why_it_matters: The 500-vs-409 split depends on whether this request created the flag. `AppRegistry.flag_needs_restart` returns that bool, but `flag_instance_needs_restart` drops it (returns None), and the settle paths return only an exception or nothing. Without threading it, the build would have to compare registry state before and after, which is the inference D1 removes. The Assumed "Carried from parent D6" bullet says every registry write for a key happens under the key lock, but `shutdown_all` runs `shutdown_instances` with no lock at process exit while an HTTP stop may still be in `shutdown_instance`. If the exit path flags first, the request reports already-flagged (409) instead of newly flagged (500). That only happens at exit, so the response may never be delivered, but the assumption is wrong as written.
findings.chosen: Make `flag_instance_needs_restart` return the registry's bool, thread it into the outcome, and add it to D1's signature inventory. Reword the D6 Assumed bullet to "every registry write for a key happens under its lock, except process-exit teardown (`shutdown_all`)".

findings.title: Moving the refusal log to callers makes a silent refusal the default for any caller that misses it
findings.why_it_matters: Today the gate logs every refusal itself, so every caller is covered by construction. After the change, a caller that discards the returned outcomes refuses silently, which breaks "no silent states". The ledger names the right sites (`_start_for_restart`, `apply_changes`'s autostart loop, `start_apps`). The critic's claim that the `restart.indices` path and `bootstrap_apps` are missing is overstated: `create_one` lives inside `_start_for_restart`, and `bootstrap_apps` goes through `start_apps`. The fragility still holds, though. `_start_for_restart` has two branches, `create_one` runs in an `asyncio.gather` that discards returns, and `start_apps`' gather currently inspects only exceptions. Each has to log, and nothing checks that they do.
findings.chosen: Add to the D12 Assumed bullet: every no-channel caller logs refusals through one shared helper (for example `log_refusals(outcomes)`), and a test proves a refused index through `apply_changes` (both `_start_for_restart` branches) and through `bootstrap_apps` emits exactly one ERROR.

findings.title: The wire outcome entry doesn't define its valid `result`/`needs_restart` pairs, what `needs_restart` means, or how to treat an unknown `result`
findings.why_it_matters: The entry has two orthogonal fields, but after D2/D3 only some pairs occur: `succeeded`/false, `failed`/true (this request flagged it) or false (a plain failure), and `refused`/true. `succeeded` + `needs_restart: true` is impossible (D2-B was rejected), and `refused` + false is unspecified. `needs_restart` reads as "flagged after this request" for `failed` and "flagged before it" for `refused`, and the ledger doesn't say which it means. `result` is an open literal, so a later value (for example `skipped`) needs a client rule. Without one, a client branching on `needs_restart` alone, or treating an unknown `result` as success, gets it wrong. Published valid pairs become de facto contract either way, so they should be stated deliberately.
findings.chosen: In D2's shared text, which carries into the wire model docstring, state the valid pairs (`succeeded`/false; `failed`/true or false; `refused`/true, the only refusal today). Define `needs_restart` as "this index is flagged needs-restart after this request". State that a client treats an unknown `result` as "don't assume success".

findings.title: The 202→200 change misses several 202 references the build would leave stale
findings.why_it_matters: The Summary's touch list names the frontend comment and mocks but not the server side: the route decorator, the six route docstrings ("Returns 202 once the start is accepted"), the other in-module docstrings that mention a 202, and the `exceptions.py` comment about "a lying 202". The route docstrings become the published OpenAPI descriptions. The scheduler route keeps its 202, so a blanket replace would be wrong.
findings.chosen: Add the apps.py decorator and docstrings and the exceptions.py:320 comment to the Summary's Status-mapping and Frontend bullets, and note that the scheduler route's 202 is intentionally unchanged.

findings.title: A newer CLI against an older server reports "version skew" after the action already ran
findings.why_it_matters: D4 makes `outcomes` required and relies on the floor bump, but the CLI never calls `check_server_version`. A CLI pointed with `--server-url` at a server one release behind posts a start/stop/reload that succeeds (202, no `outcomes`), then fails to parse the body. `handle_malformed_response` words that as "Check --server-url and for CLI/server version skew" and exits 1. For `reload`, a user who retries reloads twice. The client library's `ResponseValidationError` docstring already says a 2xx means the server acted, but the CLI's wording doesn't.
findings.recommended: A: Specify that the CLI's malformed-response handling for an action endpoint's 2xx says the action may have run and to check `hassette app list` before retrying.
findings.chosen: B: Accept as a known limitation: a newer CLI against an older server reports version skew after the action has already run.

findings.title: HTTP refusals and outcome-built failures leave no route-level server log line
findings.why_it_matters: Audience assumption: an operator who debugs from the server log rather than from the client. The design deletes `_raise_if_target_failed`, which today logs a WARNING per failed action, and `http_exception_handler` logs nothing for a `WebApiError`. After the change, a 409 refusal or a 500 built from outcomes leaves no route-level line saying who asked for what. The underlying states are still logged in the lifecycle layer (the flag-time ERROR, init failures, stop timeouts), so what's missing is the request record, not the cause. The Posture's "a refusal is reported once: in the response on HTTP" chose this.
findings.recommended: B: Accept as a known limitation: a failed or refused HTTP action leaves only the lifecycle-layer log of its cause, with no route-level line naming the request.
findings.chosen: B: Accept as a known limitation: a failed or refused HTTP action leaves only the lifecycle-layer log of its cause, with no route-level line naming the request.

findings.title: `ProblemDetail.outcomes` puts an app-action member on every error schema
findings.why_it_matters: Audience assumption: an open-source library with a published OpenAPI consumed by generated clients. `ProblemDetail` is returned for every web API error. Adding `outcomes: list[AppActionOutcome] | None` makes every error response in the OpenAPI document, and the frontend's `RawErrorBody` keyed on `ProblemDetail`, carry an app-specific member, and pulls the app outcome model into the generic problems module. It's additive and optional, so released clients don't break. It matters only when a second route family wants per-item results.
findings.recommended: B: Accept as a known limitation: every problem body's schema carries an optional app-action `outcomes` member until a second route family needs per-item results.
findings.chosen: B: Accept as a known limitation: every problem body's schema carries an optional app-action `outcomes` member until a second route family needs per-item results.

findings.title: Findings converge on `_settle_stop_outcomes`' after-the-fact inference
findings.why_it_matters: Findings 2 and 3 come from different critics and both land on `_settle_stop_outcomes`. After the teardown, that step decides outcomes for every target in the collector. It treats a target with no recorded outcome as "already stopped", and it reads the registry to decide refusals. Finding 2 is the scope problem: a per-index stop settles its siblings too. Finding 3 is the default problem: a missing record means success on stop but failure on start and reload. Both come from settle *inferring* an outcome after the fact instead of being told one. That cuts against D1's deciding factor ("each outcome is a recorded fact of this request, not inferred"). Should the stop settle step be re-evaluated as a mechanism (whether it needs to infer at all, or whether these are limitations to accept and document) rather than patched twice?
findings.recommended: A: Re-evaluate `_settle_stop_outcomes` before addressing Findings 2 and 3 individually. Open questions: should "already stopped" be decided from what was true when the targets were chosen, or from what the teardown recorded? Whose indices should a per-index stop settle? Should a stop target with no record fail closed like start and reload? Or is today's inference an acceptable, documented limitation?
findings.chosen: A: Re-evaluate _settle_stop_outcomes before addressing Findings 2 and 3 individually

findings.title: A per-index stop settles every target, so it stamps mid-stop siblings "already stopped"
findings.why_it_matters: `_stop_instance_unlocked` stops one index but ends with `_settle_stop_outcomes(app_key, outcomes)`, which loops over every target in the collector. On a config change that restarts instances A and B of one app, `_stop_for_restart` gathers both per-index stops over one shared collector. When A finishes first, its settle step writes `succeeded`, "already stopped", into B's slot while B is still tearing down, and marks B decided. If B's shutdown then raises unexpectedly, `fail_undecided` skips B because it is already decided, so B stays `succeeded` even though its stop raised. Today only `log_refusals` reads that collector, so nobody sees the result. Anyone who later reads the apply_changes collector will.
findings.recommended: B: Accept as a known limitation: during a multi-index config restart, a sibling's settle step can stamp a still-stopping instance "already stopped", and that value survives if the instance's own shutdown raises. Only `log_refusals` reads it.
findings.chosen: Superseded by Finding 1

findings.title: Stop infers "already stopped" from a missing outcome, the opposite default from start and reload
findings.why_it_matters: For start and reload, `finish()` fails any slot still undecided (fail-closed). For stop, `_settle_stop_outcomes` runs before `finish` and turns every undecided, unflagged slot into `succeeded`, "already stopped" (fail-open). Today every teardown path in `shutdown_instance` records explicitly, and the exception path calls `fail_undecided` first, so the default never fires for a running instance. A future teardown path that forgets to record would report a still-running instance as stopped with a 200. That is the "lying 200" this spec removes. (The critic's second point, an exit-time flag landing between teardown and settle, is already accepted under parent D6 in the Assumed section, so it is not repeated here.)
findings.chosen: Superseded by Finding 1

findings.title: D1 says "a slot is written at most once per phase", but the collector is last-writer-wins
findings.why_it_matters: D1 states "A slot is written at most once per phase", and the finish step fills only empty slots. `ActionOutcomes._write` does something else: a later write in the same half replaces an earlier one (its docstring: "A later write replaces an earlier one, with two exceptions for a reload"). The only protection is the newly-flagged early return. This happens by design. For example, a stop's settle step overrides a teardown's outcome with `refused` for a flagged index. The Build "Calls made" section doesn't record the divergence, so a reader of the ledger will trust an invariant the code doesn't keep.
findings.chosen: Add one line to the ledger's Build "Calls made during the build" list: within a half, a later write replaces an earlier one, except that a failure that newly flagged the index stands. A stop's settle step relies on this to record `refused` over a teardown outcome. The D1 body stays as ratified.

findings.title: A start or stop with no targets answers 200 with `outcomes: []`
findings.why_it_matters: D1 and Build call 2 treat "a 200 with an empty list" as a bug, but only close it for a vanished manifest. A manifest whose `app_config` normalizes to zero instances (`normalize_app_config` maps `None`, and an empty list, to `[]`) gives `start_app` no targets. `_stop_app_unlocked` logs "Cannot stop app ..., not found" and returns. `finish()` returns `()`, `_problem_code_for(())` is `None`, and the route answers 200 with `outcomes: []`. `outcomes` is required on the published contract and documented as "one entry per instance the action targeted", so a client can't tell "nothing to do" from "nothing happened". `stop_app`'s own "not found" warning shows the code treats this case as an error. The compat harness also invents a succeeded entry for apps with no instances, so the real server's empty list is never exercised there.
findings.recommended: B: Accept as a known limitation: an action on an app that configures zero instances answers 200 with an empty `outcomes` list.
findings.chosen: B: Accept as a known limitation: an action on an app that configures zero instances answers 200 with an empty `outcomes` list.

findings.title: A whole-app start or reload that raises mid-initialization reports `failed` but leaves registered, never-initialized instances that the next start calls "already running"
findings.why_it_matters: When something raises, the per-instance path shuts the phantom down (`_create_instance_unlocked`'s `except`, which calls `shutdown_instance(phantom, cause=exc)`). The whole-app path has no such cleanup. `create_instances` has already registered every new instance. A raise before or during `initialize_instances` (the NOT_STARTED `send_event` loop, or a raise from a sibling's failure handling) escapes to `start_app`/`reload_app`'s `except`, and `finish(reason)` marks those slots `failed`. The registry still holds those instances, so a later start sees them as live and reports `succeeded`, "already running", without anything having initialized. On `main` the same path also had no cleanup (its `start_app` had no catch at all; the phantom handling exists only in `_create_instance_unlocked`). So the registry divergence was already there, but the new outcome vocabulary now states it in the response.
findings.recommended: B: Accept as a known limitation: if hassette itself raises partway through a whole-app start, the instances it registered but never initialized stay registered. The response says `failed`, and a later start reports them "already running" until a stop or reload clears them.
findings.chosen: B: Accept as a known limitation: if hassette itself raises partway through a whole-app start, the instances it registered but never initialized stay registered. The response says `failed`, and a later start reports them "already running" until a stop or reload clears them.

findings.title: A reload of a blocked app hides its stop half's failure from `detail`
findings.why_it_matters: `reload_app` runs the stop half, then `_start_app_unlocked` raises `AppBlockedError(outcomes=outcomes.snapshot())`. `_await_operation` answers 409 `app_blocked` with the fixed detail "App ... is blocked by the --app filter". D6 says that 409 carries the stop half's outcomes in the body, and it does. But D3 says the `detail` of a 409 or 500 from an app action names every instance that didn't succeed, because the CLI and the toast read only `detail`. A stop half that created a zombie (`failed` plus `needs_restart`) therefore shows the user only "blocked by --app". The flag-time ERROR log and the apps-page badge still show the zombie.
findings.recommended: B: Accept as a known limitation: a reload of a blocked app whose stop half failed reports only "blocked by the --app filter" in `detail`. The failure is visible in `problem.outcomes`, the apps-page badge and the server log.
findings.chosen: B: Accept as a known limitation: a reload of a blocked app whose stop half failed reports only "blocked by the --app filter" in `detail`. The failure is visible in `problem.outcomes`, the apps-page badge and the server log.

findings.title: An unexpected raise early in a reload's create half overwrites a flagged index's `refused` with a plain `failed`
findings.why_it_matters: In a reload, the stop half's `_settle_stop_outcomes` writes `refused` (`needs_restart: true`) for an already-flagged index. `begin_create_half` then removes that index from `_decided`. If something raises after that and before the create-half gate re-records the refusal, `finish(reason)` calls `fail_undecided`, which writes `failed` with `needs_restart: false`. `_write`'s only protection is for newly-flagged failures, so the refused slot is replaced. Examples are `_emit_discarded_entry_events`' `send_event`, or the prune step in `_start_app_unlocked` before `create_instances`. The response then says 500 `failed` and `needs_restart: false` for an instance the registry still flags. That breaks D2's valid-pairs rule ("`needs_restart` means this index is flagged after this request"). The senior critic proposed Auto-apply. This synthesis classifies it User-directed because the fix adds a rule by which `_write` guesses from an earlier slot.
findings.recommended: B: Accept as a known limitation: if hassette raises early in a reload's create half, an already-flagged index reports `failed` with `needs_restart: false` (500 instead of 409) for that one request. The registry flag stays correct.
findings.chosen: B: Accept as a known limitation: if hassette raises early in a reload's create half, an already-flagged index reports `failed` with `needs_restart: false` (500 instead of 409) for that one request. The registry flag stays correct.

findings.title: `stop_app` and `stop_instance` don't wrap their locked bodies, so Build call 5's "every public method catches" overstates
findings.why_it_matters: Build call 5 removes `_await_operation`'s `ValueError`/`RuntimeError` → `action_failed` mapping because D5 "has every public lifecycle method catch and record unexpected exceptions". `start_app`, `reload_app`, `start_instance` and `reload_instance` wrap their bodies. `stop_app` and `stop_instance` don't: their inner `_stop_*_unlocked` catch the teardown, but `_outcomes_for`, `_settle_stop_outcomes` and `finish()` run outside any catch. If one of those raised after the stop ran, the route would answer 500 `internal_error` with no outcomes for instances that really were stopped. That is the option D5 rejected. The senior critic adds that `_outcomes_for` and `_require_manifest` run before the `try` in the start methods too. Nothing there can raise today. Note that `_settle_stop_outcomes` iterates `outcomes.indices`, so `_write`'s non-target `ValueError` can't fire from it.
findings.recommended: B: Accept as a known limitation: a bookkeeping bug in a stop's settle or finish step would reach the route as a 500 `internal_error` without outcomes. Build call 5's reason holds only for start and reload.
findings.chosen: B: Accept as a known limitation: a bookkeeping bug in a stop's settle or finish step would reach the route as a 500 `internal_error` without outcomes. Build call 5's reason holds only for start and reload.

findings.title: A reload whose create half fails drops the stop half's failure from `reason`
findings.why_it_matters: `_write` appends `STOP_FAILED_PREFIX` + the stop half's reason only when the create half *succeeds*. When the stop timed out without flagging and the create then fails (a class-load error, for example), `reason` carries only the create failure, and the stop failure survives only in the server log. The status is 500 either way, so detail is lost but the status is right. This matches D6's text ("the create half decides"). D6 ratified losing the clean-timeout signal from the status when the create half succeeds. It didn't address the reason when the create half fails.
findings.chosen: Side B: Prefix the stop failure on a failing create half too

findings.title: The collector's non-target `ValueError` can abort teardown bookkeeping before the STOPPED event
findings.why_it_matters: `_write` raises `ValueError` for an index that isn't a target. `shutdown_instance` calls `outcomes.succeeded(instance_index)` after teardown and before `send_outcome_event`. If a caller ever passed a collector without that index, the STOPPED event would never be sent and the WS status cache would stay on STOPPING. A validity check on request bookkeeping would then break the telemetry path it only observes. Every current caller targets its indices, so this can't happen today.
findings.chosen: Side A: Keep the raise

findings.title: The `needs_restart` docstrings say "nothing was done", though the app's other instances were acted on
findings.why_it_matters: Audience assumption: scripted or library callers of the open-source client who branch on exception family. Under D3, any whole-app action on an app with one flagged instance answers 409 `needs_restart`, even though the siblings really were stopped, started or reloaded. The `ProblemCode.NEEDS_RESTART` docstring and the `NeedsRestartError` docstring say "so nothing was done to it", meaning the flagged instance, and are silent about the siblings. Elsewhere in the 409 family, `ActionInProgressError` and `AppBlockedError` really do mean nothing ran. `python-client.md` already says "The app's other instances were still acted on" and tells callers that retry on `ConflictError` to catch `NeedsRestartError` first. `NeedsRestartError` already says "Not retryable". So the remaining gap is the in-code docstrings an IDE user reads.
findings.recommended: B: Accept as a known limitation: the in-code docstrings describe only the flagged instance. `python-client.md` documents the sibling effect and the retry guidance.
findings.chosen: B: Accept as a known limitation: the in-code docstrings describe only the flagged instance. `python-client.md` documents the sibling effect and the retry guidance.

findings.title: `--json` failure output drops the per-instance outcomes the server returned
findings.why_it_matters: The CLI's `--json` output is the contract for shell scripts. On success, `hassette app start|stop|reload --json` adds `outcomes`, all `succeeded` by construction. On 409 or 500, `handle_http_error` reads only `detail` and `_write_json_error` writes it. The problem body's `outcomes` never reach stdout except inside the raw `body` under `--debug`. A script that wants to know which instance failed has to parse the prose `detail`. Build call 9 records "Error output stays the CLI's standard error document" but gives no reason beyond Posture's "no per-instance view", and that Posture line is about a human view, not a machine passthrough.
findings.recommended: A: When a 409/500 problem body carries `outcomes`, include them in the CLI's `--json` error document.
findings.chosen: A: When a 409/500 problem body carries outcomes, include them in the CLI's --json error document

findings.title: The CLI docs read as if `--json` failure output carries `outcomes`
findings.why_it_matters: `docs/pages/cli/commands.md:125` says "When it fails or is refused on any instance, the command prints the error ... and exits 1. With `--json`, the printed object adds an `outcomes` list". Read in order, the second sentence seems to describe the failure output, but only the success object carries `outcomes`. A script author will expect per-instance data on failure and not find it.
findings.chosen: Reword line 125 to say the `--json` success object adds an `outcomes` list, and the failure output is the standard error document whose `detail` names each instance that didn't succeed. If Finding 13 is resolved with option A, describe the error document's `outcomes` instead.

findings.title: The web UI still offers Start and Reload on a flagged instance, and those can only answer 409
findings.why_it_matters: Audience assumption: a UI user with a flagged instance. A flagged instance shows status FAILED, `CAN_START.failed` is true, so Start and Reload stay clickable, and they now always answer 409 `needs_restart`. Before this branch the same click answered a generic 500 (#3110). The toast text is better now, but the button still leads nowhere. The frontend already has `needs_restart` per instance in its app data and store, but `action-buttons.tsx` doesn't gate on it. Posture scoped the frontend to "toast reads detail", so this is outside the ratified scope.
findings.recommended: A: File a follow-up issue to disable or relabel Start/Reload for an instance with `needs_restart` set.
findings.chosen: A: File a follow-up issue to disable or relabel Start/Reload for an instance with needs_restart set

findings.title: Config-change restarts log stop-half refusals as "Not starting", contradicting the ledger's last Build note
`--json` success object silently loses `status`, and the CLI doesn't warn about version skew
Compat-list handling is unverified for the removed `ActionResponse.status` property
Every problem body's schema now carries `outcomes`, and `wire` gains an intra-package import from `problems` to `apps`
A whole-app start or reload reports `succeeded` when post-ready reconcile raised, while the per-instance path shuts the instance down
